q: The town museum is open from ten in the morning to five in the evening every day except Monday. Tickets cost 100 rupees for adults and 30 rupees for students who show a college card. Children under five enter free. Visitors may take photographs in the main hall, but not in the coin gallery, where the lights are kept low to protect the old metal. According to the passage, where are photographs NOT allowed?
x: The passage says photographs are allowed in the main hall but not in the coin gallery. The other places are not described as having any ban.

q: To make kheer for six people, wash half a cup of rice and soak it for an hour. Then boil it slowly in a litre of milk for forty minutes, stirring often so that it does not stick. Add sugar and cardamom and cook for ten minutes more. Finally, let the kheer cool for two hours before serving it, topped with chopped almonds. According to the passage, how long does it take from the start of soaking until the kheer is ready to serve?
x: Soaking 1 hour + boiling 40 minutes + cooking 10 minutes + cooling 2 hours = 3 hours 50 minutes. Leaving out the ten extra minutes of cooking gives the tempting 3 hours 40 minutes.

q: Many people believe that a camel stores water in its hump, but the hump is really a store of fat. When food is short, the camel uses this fat for energy, and the hump becomes smaller and may even flop to one side. A camel can lose a quarter of its body weight in water and still survive, and when it finds water it can drink more than a hundred litres in a few minutes. Which statement is supported by the passage?
o: A camel's hump stores water for long journeys
A camel's hump gets smaller when the camel uses its stored fat
A camel dies if it loses a quarter of its body weight in water
A camel needs several hours to drink a hundred litres
x: The passage says the camel uses the fat in its hump when food is short, and the hump becomes smaller. It states the hump holds fat, not water, and that the camel survives losing a quarter of its weight in water.

q: The college's annual sports day will be held on 15 March. Students who wish to take part must give their names to Mr Khalid by 1 March. No student may enter more than two events. The races will begin at 8:30 a.m., and prizes will be given at 1 p.m. by the chief guest. According to the notice, by what date must students give their names?
x: Names must reach Mr Khalid by 1 March. The 15th of March is the date of the sports day itself.

q: Last Friday the medical students held a blood donation camp in the college hall. Donors had to be between eighteen and sixty years old and weigh at least fifty kilograms. Each donor's haemoglobin was checked first. Seventy-two people came, but twelve were turned away, most of them because their haemoglobin was too low. Every donor was given juice and biscuits and asked to rest for fifteen minutes. Which statement is NOT true according to the passage?
o: Sixty people gave blood at the camp
Most of the people turned away were under eighteen
Donors had to weigh at least fifty kilograms
Each donor's haemoglobin was checked first
x: The passage says most of those turned away had low haemoglobin, not that they were too young. Seventy-two came and twelve were turned away, so sixty gave blood.

q: During its book fair week, a bookshop gives 20 per cent off any book priced above 500 rupees and 10 per cent off every other book. Bags are free, but gift-wrapping costs 50 rupees a book. Sara buys a dictionary priced at 800 rupees and two story books priced at 300 rupees each, and asks for only the dictionary to be gift-wrapped. According to the passage, how much does Sara pay in all?
x: Dictionary: 800 less 20% = 640. Story books: 300 less 10% = 270 each, so 540. Adding 50 rupees for wrapping one book gives 640 + 540 + 50 = 1,230 rupees.

q: Residents of Block C are informed that the water supply will be shut off from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. on Thursday while workers replace the main pipe. Please store enough water on Wednesday night. Tankers will stand near the park gate for emergencies only. We regret the trouble and thank you for your patience. The main purpose of this notice is to:
o: Ask residents to pay for a new main water pipe
Invite residents to a meeting near the park gate
Complain that residents of Block C waste water
Tell residents about a planned water shut-off and how to prepare for it
x: The notice gives the time of the shut-off and advises residents to store water. It asks for no payment, calls no meeting and makes no complaint.

q: On the morning of her chemistry practical, Fatima woke early and revised her notes on titration. After breakfast she checked that her lab coat and calculator were in her bag. On the way to college she realised she had left her roll-number slip at home, so she phoned her brother, who brought it on his motorbike. She reached the laboratory ten minutes before the start. Why did Fatima phone her brother?
o: She was late and needed a lift
She had left her roll-number slip at home
She had left her lab coat at home
x: The passage says she phoned her brother because she had left her roll-number slip at home. She had already checked that her lab coat and calculator were in her bag, and she arrived early.

q: A college asked 200 of its students how they travel to classes. Ninety said they walk, sixty come by bus and thirty ride motorbikes. All the others are dropped off by car. Of the bus users, one third said the buses are often late. According to the passage, how many students are dropped off by car?
x: 90 + 60 + 30 = 180 students use the other ways, so 200 - 180 = 20 are dropped off by car.

q: When the results were announced, the hockey team was jubilant. The players lifted their coach onto their shoulders, danced around the ground and sang all the way back to the hostel. Even the quietest boy on the team was shouting and laughing. As used in the passage, 'jubilant' means:
x: Dancing, singing and shouting with laughter show great happiness, so 'jubilant' means full of joy. 'Quietly proud' does not fit such noisy celebration.

q: Grandfather was obstinate about his old radio. His children bought him a new one with clear sound and a remote control, but he left it in its box. Every evening he sat with the old set, turning its knob and shaking it when the signal faded, and he refused to hear a word against it. As used in the passage, 'obstinate' means:
x: He keeps the old radio and refuses to listen to any criticism of it, so 'obstinate' means stubborn, unwilling to change his mind. Nothing in the passage shows he is afraid of the new set.

q: After two nights of little sleep, Hamza felt lethargic in the morning lectures. He yawned, his eyes kept closing, and when the teacher asked him a question he answered slowly, as if every word were heavy. He did not even feel like walking to the canteen at break. As used in the passage, 'lethargic' means:
x: Yawning, closing eyes, slow answers and no wish to walk all point to having no energy. Lack of sleep, not boredom, is given as the cause.

q: Bilal's mother came back into the kitchen and stopped. The fish she had left on the table to cool was gone. A trail of small bones led from the table to the sofa, where the family cat lay on a cushion, slowly licking its whiskers. What can be inferred from the passage?
o: Someone had put the fish in the fridge
A visitor had taken the fish away
The cat had eaten the fish
x: The trail of bones leads to the cat, which is licking its whiskers, so the clues point to the cat. Nothing in the passage mentions Bilal, the fridge or a visitor.

q: Sometimes I still walk past the school where I learnt to read. The mulberry tree in the yard is gone, and a car park stands where we once played marbles, but I can almost hear the bell and the chanting of tables through the open windows. How short those afternoons seemed then, and how long ago they are now. The writer's mood in this passage is:
x: The writer fondly remembers the past and feels it is now far away, which is nostalgia. There is no anger at the changes, and the writer clearly cares, so 'indifferent' is wrong.

q: The stray dog had been chased and beaten by boys many times. When Ayesha first knelt down and held out a piece of bread, it was hostile: it backed away, bared its teeth and growled. Only after she had visited it every day for two weeks did it begin to wag its tail when it saw her. As used in the passage, 'hostile' means:
x: Backing away, baring its teeth and growling show an unfriendly, threatening attitude. Its later tail-wagging shows the change from hostility to trust.

q: The surgeon's face was grave as he came out of the operating theatre. He took off his mask slowly, asked the family to sit down, and spoke in a low voice about the next forty-eight hours. Hamza's mother held his hand tightly. As used in the passage, 'grave' means:
x: Here 'grave' is an adjective describing a face: his low voice and the family's fear show it means serious. 'Burial place' is the meaning of the noun 'grave', which does not fit this sentence.

q: Ali's aunt kept her best china plates in a glass cabinet and never used them, not even at Eid. When Ali asked why, she smiled and said the plates had come with her from her mother's house fifty years ago, and that every chip would feel like losing a piece of her mother. Why does Ali's aunt not use the plates?
o: They are too small for serving a large family
She bought them recently and is saving them
They remind her of her mother and she fears damaging them
x: She links the plates to her mother and says a chip would feel like a loss, so she protects them. They are fifty years old, not new, and no chips are mentioned.

q: Years later, Sara still had a vivid memory of her first day at medical college: the smell of the new white coat, the long echoing corridors, the nervous laughter of the girls beside her, and the exact words of the professor's welcome. As used in the passage, 'vivid' means:
x: Sara remembers smells, sounds and exact words, so her memory is clear and detailed. 'Faint and unclear' is the opposite.

q: When the coach read out the team for the final, Hamza's name was not on the list. He said nothing, packed his kit slowly, and told his friends he had a headache and wanted to go home. That evening his mother found his new football boots pushed to the very back of the cupboard. What does the passage suggest?
o: Hamza was too ill to play in the final
Hamza was deeply disappointed at not being chosen
Hamza had decided to buy better boots
Hamza did not care about the final
x: His silence, slow packing and hidden boots show hurt at being left out; the headache is an excuse to leave. Hiding the boots shows he cared, so 'did not care' is wrong.

q: "A deafening silence filled the ward as the surgeon walked in." The phrase 'deafening silence' is an example of:
x: An oxymoron puts two opposite ideas side by side; silence cannot literally be deafening. There is no comparison with 'like' or 'as', so it is not a simile.

q: "The rough bark scraped her palms, and the icy stream numbed her bare feet." The imagery in this line mainly appeals to the sense of:
x: Rough bark scraping the palms and icy water numbing the feet are both felt through the skin, so the imagery appeals to touch.

q: In which sentence is hyperbole used?
o: "This bag weighs a ton; I can hardly lift it."
"The bag was as heavy as a sack of wheat."
"The heavy bag groaned at its seams."
"The bag was heavy, so Ali carried it slowly."
x: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration: a bag one can carry does not really weigh a ton. The 'as heavy as' line is a simile, the 'groaned' line is personification, and the last is literal.

q: "Hope is a lamp the traveller keeps, / Burning low while the desert sleeps." What does the poet suggest about hope?
o: It is dangerous, like fire in a dry desert
It goes out completely when night comes
It gives quiet guidance and comfort in hard times
It belongs only to people who travel
x: The metaphor compares hope to a lamp that keeps burning in the dark, lonely desert, so hope guides and comforts in hard times. The lamp keeps burning, so it does not go out at night.

q: "The traffic police officer was fined for parking his car in a no-parking zone." This sentence is an example of:
x: It is irony because the result is the opposite of what we expect: the man who enforces parking rules breaks one himself. There is no comparison or exaggeration.

q: Which line contains both alliteration and a simile?
o: "The tired traveller trudged up the hill."
"The tired traveller trudged on like a turtle."
"Our guest walked as slowly as a tortoise."
"The path was a ribbon of silver."
x: 'Tired traveller trudged ... turtle' repeats the 't' sound, and 'like a turtle' is a simile. The second line has only alliteration, the third only a simile, and the last is a metaphor.

q: The poet writes, "Time is a thief that steals our years." What idea does this line express?
o: Time passes more slowly as we grow old
People waste their time on useless things
Time quietly takes away our life and youth
Most thefts take place late at night
x: The metaphor compares time to a thief: our years slip away from us without our noticing, as a thief takes things secretly. The line says nothing about time slowing down or wasting time.
